utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I'd like to introduce to the Chamber Ethan Notarius from Buffalo, New York. He's joining us this session. He's working as a legal intern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wanted to begin by asking about one of the commemorations of the liberation of Zvornik, in this case the anniversary of the event that was called the anniversary of the liberation of Zvornik which was held on 9 April 1994. I'll show you a couple of pictures about that, okay? Do you generally recall that such an event occurred or events of that type occurred on the anniversary of April 9th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible. I don't remember the exact year but it may have happened that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's take a look at a couple of pictures initially.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we can go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For example, you can show him the very next page. What does it say, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This says solemn session of the Zvornik municipal assembly on the occasion of the day of the liberation of Zvornik, the 9th of April, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay, and if we could -- I just wanted to turn to find -- to identify some of the other persons present. If we could turn to page 15, please. And do you recognise that person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Brano Grujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And I believe the next page will have what's handwritten on the back. Which should state Brano Grujic president of the municipality giving a speech at the ceremony on the occasion of the second anniversary of Zvornik's liberation and also dated 9 April 1994. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And for identification purposes, this is marked ERN 04452465 and the previous -- the photograph was 2464. Okay? And if we can turn next to e-court page 19. Do you recognise that gentleman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The face is familiar, but I cannot remember the man exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at the next page. There are about four or five photographs of this gentleman in the collection of photographs about this event. And as we see here again dated 9 April 1994, Zvornik, the handwritten notation, Radmilo Bogdanovic. Does that refresh your recollection that the gentleman depicted here at the event is the minister of the interior of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's him, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And finally if we could turn to e-court page 11, and do you recognise this man depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one in the picture is Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And are you able to see - we can blow it up - what his name tag says?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "host."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we turn to the next page, again indicating the same date, and stating in handwritten, Zeljo Raznatovic, aka Arkan, at the ceremonial session of the Zvornik Municipal Assembly on the occasion of the Zvornik liberation day; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that one is marked 04452461 and the photograph is 04452460. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender those photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we don't have any objection to the photographs that were discussed with the witness being admitted with the exception of page 7 which we don't think the witness was able to comment on at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I think in fairness, the witness understood it takes place at the municipal -- well, I'd have to go back into private session to argue that, but I think the comments were sufficient given the context as we understand it and what we know about the witness's roles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will admit those shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6371, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, yesterday we spoke a bit about Marko Pavlovic, the commander of the TO, beginning in April, and it's -- this trial -- and let me step back. We talked about -- a bit about Arkan's men and there were -- I think there was reference yesterday in a more general fashion to other paramilitary personnel in Zvornik at the time. This Trial Chamber has received evidence including payroll records of the TO reflecting that a group known as Zuco's units, which was sometimes referred to as the Yellow Wasps but more formally known as the Igor Markovic unit, were part of the TO and were outfitted and received payment from the TO. For that we could turn to P2867, P2863, D1417 and others. Now, as you previously acknowledged it was the Zvornik municipal authorities, that is the interim or provisional government that financed the TO; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you were aware at the time that the paramilitary -- so-called paramilitaries were in fact financed by and on the TO payroll; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I supposed as much but only when I saw these documents, I said that this was possible. It was a real possibility because they were on the list of the TO as volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I think you said at page 28 of your -- in 2002, of your statement, that you were aware that when money was given to Marko Pavlovic, finance would also go to these paramilitary groups and that it was "in disputable that they had this support. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. And if we could quickly turn to 65 ter 18748 and turn, please, to the last page of the English and the second-to-last page of the B/C/S, just looking at the -- okay, let's -- let's -- just looking at the last paragraph, sir, the -- if we just turn to that last paragraph, that indicates that -- in the last two paragraphs of the document -- that on -- first of all, let me indicate what the document is. It's a document from the federal secretariat for the National Defence security administration. It is dated as we see on the front page, 26 May 1992, contains information about various crimes. It's a military secret, highly confidential. And then as we turn to the last page we see the following entries, on 28 April this year four members of the Zvornik municipal TO who are under the command of Zuco killed two Muslim men and raped two Muslim women, and then the next entry is reflects events of 2 May of 1992, indicating that the commander of the Zvornik municipal TO, Marko Pavlovic, informed the OB of the execution of 19 residents of Muslim nationality from the village of Snagovo. So this document, in particular the entry of 28 April, reflects the understanding of the authorities across the river that the Zuco's units were members of the Zvornik municipality TO, correct, which is consistent with what your understanding was?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'd like to object. He's putting too many propositions to the witness at one time. It's going to be very confusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me do it this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we deal with the nature of this document first, Mr. -- whose document this is?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Witness, we can look at the front page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Witness, you can see that this is a document of the federal secretariat for the National Defence security administration and you also see the date of the document toward the bottom, and as I say, I wanted to -- wasn't directing your attention to other parts of the document but to the last two paragraphs, and in particular, to simplify the question, wanted you to confirm that the SSNO's understanding and information that the -- that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you first confirm SSNO of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is the federal secretariat for the National Defence security administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Of Yugoslavia or Serbia, Republika Srpska? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's submitted to Panic so that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, which body this is? And would you accept that based on the title, it is a body of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, it didn't exist at the time. It could only have been a body of the SFRY, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And turning to the last two paragraphs that I directed your attention to, that information that is that persons under the command of Zuco were members of the Zvornik municipality TO that's consistent with your information, isn't it, about their relationship to the TO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We must distinguish two things here. You're trying to impose something on me. I said that it was possible that they were receiving their pay because the provisional government funded the Territorial Defence. When Marko Pavlovic got money, it can't be ruled out that he also paid paramilitaries. I cannot say now what the relationship was between Zuco and Marko Pavlovic because there were other volunteers too who were in the Territorial Defence on their list and under their command, and Zuco certainly was not under the command of Marko Pavlovic. That's 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would tender that document and I also tender page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I see the first page again? This is allegedly a report about the crimes committed by certain members, in the republic -- Republika Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This clear -- there is clearly a disconnect between that title and the geographic location [overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So whether Zvornik is part of RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't think there is any -- I don't think anyone is suggesting that. I think that's -- I mean, I wouldn't see the need to take that up. It's obvious that Zvornik is not part of the RSK and there is no suggestion to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we object to the admission of this document. The witness hasn't confirmed anything about the document. He hasn't -- it doesn't directly contradict him, and in particular, I call your attention to the last sentence of that paragraph which is what I think the reason why Mr. Tieger wants the document to be admitted. I don't think that we could admit a document like this which has a lot of information just on the one small sentence, whether it confirms or contradicts the witness and then have other parts of that document which are very controversial just simply be part of the record which the Chamber can use in its judgement. So we don't think that this is a sufficient foundation to admit the document through this witness. If you do want to admit something, we would ask that you admit the first sentence of paragraph 9 on the top of this last page only.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not seeking the admission of the entire document only the referenced portions which are the front -- the cover page and the last -- the last two paragraphs. Certainly agree with Mr. Robinson that the first sentence at a minimum obviously goes in. I can't even see a basis for any argument to the contrary but I continue to see that -- to maintain that there is sufficient basis for admission of those two paragraphs, in light of the issues presented to this witness in general. And the nature of the document. The rest of it, as Mr. Robinson likes to say, goes to weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you upload the English last page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, the line you're referring to begins with, "There were old men." What exactly are you objecting to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's the last sentence of the top paragraph which reads the leadership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: The leadership, okay. Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will admit the first page and the last page.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6372, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement at paragraphs -- beginning at paragraphs 51, there is a section which basically falls under the heading of movement of the population, and you mention at paragraph 55 that the Muslims of Djulici "decided to leave." And at paragraph 59 you refer to the decision of the Muslims to leave Kozluk was made by them, and so on. So I want to be clear on some of the things that were happening in Zvornik. And -- that some of the information you provided about that previously. So when you returned to Zvornik from Glinica, there were still some Muslims in town but the situation for them "was awful," right, that Muslim flats were being looted and only Muslim flats were being looted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only Muslim flats were being looted, Serbian too. But it happened more after the prisoners were released -- after Zvornik was liberated, after the 9th. Then Muslim flats were looted more than the Serbian. However, Serbian flats were also being looted before the 9th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Didn't you explain that in your building there were about 80 apartments and about half and half?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that only Muslim flats had been ransacked and looted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in my entrance. The building had four entrances, and in my entrance where there were three or four Muslim flats, those were the flats that were looted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You also said that after the attack on Zvornik town, attacks on the villages continued. For example, in Kozluk, Muslims were being "beaten and killed," they could no longer go to work, and the villages around them "were burning and their lives were very bad." That's part of the situation in Zvornik for Muslims at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you read out refers to Kozluk, I believe. As far as Zvornik is concerned, at the time, as of the 9th of April, the Serbs were in control of the town. There were perhaps Muslims --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was talking about Kozluk. I was talking about the attacks on villages after the attack on Zvornik. And I think you've just confirmed that that does refer to -- that information referred to Kozluk.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding Kozluk and the nearby villages, from the very beginning of the conflict, well, there was an all out war there from the start. We didn't have any information what was going on for at least 10 to 15 days. I didn't see any of it. However, after that, I could see torched villages on both sides and I heard from the locals that there were people being detained, beaten, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, for example, the people who -- the Muslims who remained in places like Djulici, Kozluk, Sepak were in what you described as extremely dire straits; correct? And you testified to that in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The situation was dire for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the situation was such that as you yourself emphasised previously, and did so back years ago when these events were fresher in your memory, that the Muslims of Zvornik left because they were essentially compelled to leave, they didn't -- as you said it, people in Djulici, for example, did not leave voluntarily, they went under stress and in fear.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely. No one leaves of their own free will. They move because of the circumstances. In Zvornik, before Djulici, six or seven Serbs had arrived from the environs of Tuzla and those people did not come there because they wanted to go but because the situation was such that they were forced to. Now, let me tell you about the people you mentioned. When I spoke to them, they said there was no medication, no job, no electricity, no water, there is nothing. There is firing all around. And you see houses being torched daily, Muslim and Serb houses. The front line was only 4 kilometres away and what could they expect? They said that there were about 7.000 of them in the entire area whereas only 2and a half remained. That's what I clearly remember. So at the very beginning of the conflict, many people left. Those who stayed were in a bad situation. They did not even have food. They only had the food provided to them by the nearest and closest Serb neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's talk for a moment about what you learned from members of the municipal authorities, that is what they knew about what was happening and what was related to you. And let me focus for a moment on what you learned from Kosta Eric, who was as I understand it the head of sanitation or civil protection.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Kosta Eric was -- well, I don't know exactly, but I think he was the heads of civil protection or its leadership. In any case, on one occasion he came to Glinica and he told us that on one occasion they had a possibility to go and visit places where people were detained and I think he referred to the dom, the hall in Celopek, and he said they could observe traces of human blood. That's what he told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me remind you of what you told us previously years ago when these events were fresher and see if that refreshes your recollection about what Mr. Eric told you. So, for example, you did indicate you discussed that with him on two occasions, he told you that in Celopek people were brought in, Muslims from Divic and from Djulici, and they were killed. He also told you that people were tortured there, and he said that "passers-by could hear their cries, moans and screams. They were beaten with truncheons and in other ways." That's what Mr. Eric told you at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall it in such detail but he did say that there was torture there. That is certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And with respect to the Dom Kulture in Celopek he told you that he had to clean it and had a -- to use a team of men and hired trucks and drivers to do that; right? That's what you said at page 241 of your 2003 interview.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He did mention it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you also indicated on one occasion, when you were -- when you ran into Kosta Eric along with engineer Markovic, Eric told you that they were transporting a large number of bodies and burying them into mass graves, common graves; correct? That's found at page 240 of your 2003 interview.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And he also told you that people detained at the Ekonomija farm were from -- were Muslims from villages such as, according to him, Divic and Djulici; right? That's found at page 221 of your 2003 interview.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to these people in -- these Muslims in Celopek, that is the people who were -- Eric let you know were being tortured and killed, you learned that they had been -- that they were people who had been previously held in detention at the Karakaj technical school; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were people at the technical school.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the reason they were being held at the technical school was that they had been detained by Marko Pavlovic and the TO and you learned that from, among other sources, Pavlovic himself; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And he told you that he separated out these men from the women and children for the purpose of exchanging them; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he had separated some 170 men and he wanted them exchanged for the soldiers and civilians captured in Tuzla. He also said that he had a list of those men that he sent to Tuzla in order to arrange an exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you told him, as you testified in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case, that these people weren't soldiers but -- that is the people that he had -- was holding in detention weren't soldiers but they were civilians, and Pavlovic responded angrily by telling you it wasn't up to you to tell the TO what to do; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In paragraphs 51 through 60 -- well, excuse me, we just talked about -- in paragraph 62, you state that you "later informed Presidents Karadzic and Krajisnik about what you heard about the fate of Muslims in our area," and that paragraph appears after the description of movement of the population which refers to events in Djulici, Kozluk and Sepak. I'm going to ask you a few questions about what you conveyed to the Bosnian Serb leadership and when, but first I wanted to ask you about paragraph 64 of your statement. There, you state that you did not attend the Serb Assembly on May 12th because communication was so bad that you were virtually cut off and didn't know about the meeting. Now, first of all, can you confirm that Ugljevik, Lopare, Bijeljina, Sekovici and Tuzla are all contiguous -- adjacent to Zvornik. Those are all -- those are all surrounding municipalities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn to 65 ter 00581, please. This is an attendance record from the Bosnian Serb Assembly reflecting the attendance of representatives from various municipalities including from Ugljevik, Nedjeljko Gavric; from Lopare, Dragomir Kerovic; from Bijeljina, Dragoljub Micic, Miladin Nedic, Milan Novakovic; from Sekovici, Ilija Nedjic; and from Tuzla, Milan Tesic and Milan Spasojevic. That those were -- that's an accurate summary of the municipalities those representatives were from; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And as we can see from this document, those deputies attended the session of 12 May 1992, the 16th session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6373, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, in addition to the fact that deputies from the municipalities surrounding Zvornik made it to the session -- let me go into private session for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, the frequency of those meetings was corroborated by what you explained about the number of times you advised Mr. Karadzic about what was happening in Zvornik. So, for example, as a general matter you said in your 2002 statement at page 25: "Whenever there was an opportunity I would tell Karadzic and Krajisnik what was happening in Zvornik." That was your position in 2002, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? I would like ask to be precise in terms of the year and precise time to which it refers, the question, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't think it's an inappropriate question. We are going to be getting to some very specific references in just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was your position in 2002, that whenever you had a chance you would tell Karadzic and Krajisnik what was happening in Zvornik; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My first opportunity was in August, and it was a face-to-face meeting. I saw them at Pale for the first time at the first session, after Banja Luka. However, on that occasion did I not have an opportunity to speak to them tete-a-tete.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's look very carefully then at what you said in 2002 and 2003 about specific occasions on which you informed Mr. Karadzic about what was happening in Zvornik and the specific events about which you were informing him. Now, in your 2002 interview at page 25, you said the first time you informed them was "after the situation in Kozluk." And you had explained just prior to that at page 24 that this referred an event "at the end of April 1992 or beginning of May 1992 when Muslims were prepared to leave Kozluk." And then you explained in your statement: "I told them, that is Karadzic and Krajisnik, that the people in Kozluk were prepared to leave and wanted to leave and that we persuaded them to stay." And that's at page 25 of your statement. So that was the first time; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Then you also stated that you informed -- and this is at page 25 of your 2002 interview. You informed Karadzic and Krajisnik that the Muslims of Kozluk had left, and that departure occurred in June of 1992; right? So --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: First?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First, the Muslims wanted to leave in April and May according to you and were persuaded to stay, and according to your statement you informed Karadzic and Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then the Muslims actually left in June and you informed them of that, so it's two separate occasions; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the first time, I met Krajisnik and Karadzic face to face in August 2002 about those matters. Before that, I did not have such discussions face to face with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As I mentioned that's found at page 25 of your 2002 interview. And what you said there, I'm going to quote it again: "The first time that I told them that the people were prepared to leave and wanted to leave and that we persuaded them to stay, I subsequently informed them that the people had left." Now, you also spoke and I'll be tendering those pages from the 2002 interview as well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We haven't seen this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's call it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let us see them first. Yes, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think the witness should be given a chance to comment on and to answer questions whenever Mr. Tieger makes a statement like that before moving on, otherwise he's just making closing submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is why I wanted to see them. We will not broadcast this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, page 25 of the English and B/C/S on page 23. Page 25 of the English and page 23 of the B/C/S. And the second paragraph of the English we see the portion that I quoted for you before where you indicate that you had discussions with them. Whenever there was an opportunity, you would tell them what was happening. The first time was when they were prepared to leave but didn't, and as you made clear in your statement and in your statement that was in late April, early May, and then you subsequently informed them subsequently two different times that the people had left; correct? That's what you said in 2002 back when these events were fresher in your memory.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be possible that I said so but it is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that, Mr. President, and

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then what is correct, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is correct that I spoke to Karadzic and Krajisnik face to face in August 1992, when I arrived at the commission, and then we discussed it. Before that, I sent them information through Deputy Simic and Dragan Micic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Shall we add this page to Exhibit P6369?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I intervene in the transcript? There is a matter of translation. It reads, "After the situation in Kozluk, I spoke to Karadzic and Krajisnik about what was going on." It is in the past. Whereas in the English we have the present continuous tense, [In English] "... about what was happening."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow you, Mr. -- what page, what line are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What we have on the screen, in the Serbian language, it is in the past, that is to say that he reported after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you make reference to the page and line numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 23 in Serbian, 25 in English. In English it is line -- it's the first sentence of the second paragraph actually. One is the past tense, and the other one should be the past continuous tense. In English, "about what is happening," it would have been properly translated had it said "what is happening" in Serbian, but this way it's a mistranslation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're talking about the exhibit, not the transcript? I don't see much problem in the document. If you find the translation to be problematic there is a procedure you may take. Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's turn to what you stated -- yes, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to provide an explanation, if possible. Of course, I received what you have in your hands now, and I read it. I'm saying something to you now that is very important in terms of clarifying what we are discussing now and that's why I'm telling you about it now. Mr. President, I'm here under oath and I have to tell the truth. Mr. Krajisnik, wishing to review his case, asked me to sign certain statements for him and answer certain questions for him, and he sent me some documents that speak about when it was possible that he, I, and Karadzic saw each other face to face, and he proved to me exactly that that was at that moment that I referred to. That is to say I could not speak to them face to face before -- before August 1992, but I did see Mr. Karadzic in Zvornik at the meeting that was held in the Municipal Assembly, and I saw Mico Stanisic in Sekovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And at a minimum, Witness, according to you, as we see at page 22 of today's transcript, you sent Karadzic and Krajisnik information about what was happening in Zvornik through Simic and Micic. That's what you said today. And you stated in your 2002 interview that when you told Karadzic about what was happening to the Muslims of Djulici, who had been detained at Karakaj and later killed, that he said he was familiar with the situation and that Dragan Micic had already informed him; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Micic could not have informed him about Djulici, but Dragan Micic did inform him, I know that for sure, about what happened in the beginning of 1992. Now, whether Dragan Micic could have known that he or -- that they had been killed or not, and how many had been killed, I'm not sure of that because I didn't know myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Page 26 of the 2002 statement, please, which is 22549, better go into private -- no, we don't need to go into private session for this. Okay. At the top of the page you're discussing -- again Marko Pavlovic telling you about the separation and detention of men for purposes of exchange; then your information that you learned that they had been detained, not only detained but maltreated and killed; you told Karadzic and Krajisnik about that, I told them about the moving out the following day when I went to Pale; there is a discussion about Karadzic's questions concerning that, I told him about what was happening in that area and what was the situation with the paramilitaries, he said that he was familiar with the situation and that the representative Dragan Micic from Bijeljina had already informed him. Okay. That's what you said in 2002, 11 years ago, about Mr. Karadzic being informed by Mr. Micic; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I did not talk to him at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just wanted to turn to what you said specifically on tape about what you explained to Mr. Karadzic about the fate of the people who had been detained, maltreated and killed. And you said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder whether the witness had the opportunity to read out the paragraph in full. Did you read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see where this is, which paragraph is this all about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's ensure that the witness is following.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's page 25 of the B/C/S. In approximately the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: According to this document, it says: "Karadzic said it wasn't allowed to happen, that any of our official representatives take part in pressurising people to leave. He did not support what was happening, but if the situation was so unbearable that people wanted to leave voluntarily then it was better that they survive than be killed. Thinking about the paramilitaries." What does it mean, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where is that paragraph? Which paragraph is this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's at the end of the same paragraph, but --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be of assistance? In Serbian, it's the third paragraph, the second half of the third paragraph from the top.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 30, as far as I can see, that I have here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now the cursor is on that paragraph. If it's the same system.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here what I have says, "When I heard these people were killed...," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and it's around the middle of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, there is a situation here that is confusing. What I said up here, this is what it says: "When I heard that these people were killed, I felt bad about that. I told Karadzic and Krajisnik about this, the first time I talked to them afterwards. The first time I talked to them afterwards." Further on, it says down here he said that he was aware of the situation and that he had already been informed about that by Dragan Micic. So this is different from what is being claimed that I talked to Karadzic immediately after these events. The first time I had the opportunity to talk about them I told them about him, and I told Simic when they have the opportunity to go to Pale and they had opportunities like that more often I told them to tell them about what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's be clear. First of all, I tender that but let's be -- and then I'm going to move on to another reflection of your same discussion about what you informed the leadership?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll add this page as well to Exhibit P6369 which is under seal in my understanding. Yes. Yes, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. And he further discussed the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the translation is also incorrect. The translation into English, [In English] And I told Karadzic and Krajisnik about his, means --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, are you referring to the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the exhibit was mistranslated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's not discuss the translation issue unless it is very important. Consult Mr. Robinson how to deal with those issues. For planning purpose, how much longer would you need, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, if I get -- depends on this last part. I'm certainly trying to finish by the end of this session, Mr. President. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You also discussed what you told the leadership in your 2003 taped interview and what you said then, and let's turn to page 194 of the 2003 interview - sorry about the delay - when you said, "I had informed," and this again as we see from the previous page at 193, about the people from KTS who had been taken to Celopek: "I had informed Mr. Karadzic earlier when those people were detained, and then after hearing that they were killed, I took the first opportunity to inform Karadzic that they had been killed." We can see that that's 65 ter 2250, please, page 194. And with the assistance of the usher if this could be provided to the witness, it's the B/C/S, if Mr. Robinson and Mr. Karadzic want to see it quickly. And, Witness, I'll tell you that's not the only time in your interview where you make clear there were -- that you informed Mr. Karadzic, both when you learned that they had been detained and then when you learned that they had been killed, that is two occasions. At page 210, you were asked, you were telling me you found out about the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Let's deal with this one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So, Witness, it's correct that in 2003 you stated that you informed Mr. Karadzic twice, first when people were detained and then after they were killed; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not correct. That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Two things then, first of all, you did say that; right? It's right there on tape.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I said it but it's not correct. I wasn't right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. And then you said it again at page 210, let's turn to page 210, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: It's not broadcast, no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The bottom of the page you were telling me that you found out that people were being detained at the technical school and you told Mr. Karadzic about this and you've also found out that they had been killed, and again you told Mr. Karadzic about this, and one more occasion quickly, and I'll ask you about both --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But we do not have B/C/S page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Oh, we will find that in just a moment, Mr. President. The problem is that the B/C/S is not compiled in the same manner as the -- because these are separate tapes as the English and so it's on separate documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But we have the B/C/S of 249 pages. But you don't have the reference number to the page, the correct page numbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have it as B/C/S page 5 -- excuse me, B/C/S page 4 through 5 of T 0001867 of 65 ter 22550. And again we have hard copies available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So, there, sir, you -- when asked whether you told Mr. Karadzic when you found out people were being detained and then you informed him, and then again after you found out that they had been killed you again informed him. You said, Yes. And then you continue on page 211, when you were asked whether you told Mr. Krajisnik too, you said, In the first case, yes, Krajisnik was there when I was telling Karadzic about the detention part, and on the second occasion, when I spoke to Karadzic, Krajisnik was not present, and I talked to him about it on the later occasion. So those are three separate excerpts from your taped interview in 2003, 11 years ago much closer to these events, when you explicitly indicated that you spoke to Mr. Karadzic about the events in Kozluk on two occasions -- not Kozluk, events referring to KTS. We already dealt with Kozluk before. That's what you explained 11 years ago, right, that there were -- that you advised him about people being detained and then you advised him about people being killed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Have you put your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's correct that 11 years ago, that was your position; right? You got the document right in front of you. Or do you dispute that that's what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not dispute that I said that but I was not right if I said that. The first time I saw them face to face was in August 1992. I provided all information through Branko Simic and Dragan Micic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender those portions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you identify the page numbers in English? Can you make sure to upload the correct B/C/S version as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. It's page 1 -- I think it's 193 through 194 and 210 through 211 in English and the corresponding pages in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will admit them under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6374, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Together with the first page, cover page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. One supplementary question. Mr. Witness, there are other ways to report to Mr. Karadzic other than tete-a-tete meeting. Then when you say it was only in August 1992, you had -- you met Mr. Karadzic for the first time, do you exclude that there was -- there were any other kind of meetings earlier than that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I explained it a moment ago that I saw Mr. Karadzic at the end of June at a meeting in Zvornik but I did not speak to him face to face. This was at the meeting. Now, why am I saying face to face? I'm saying that because that means that I could directly speak about a certain matter, directly, not indirectly through other persons. That is to say I spoke about that, I did not report about that or provide information because that would mean through other persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see given my effort to finish by the end of the session I'd have five minutes left, I would ask for an early break. Let me try to pare down what I've got and be as efficient as possible in the limited time I think the Court would be willing to give me, if you don't mind if that would be of some assistance, otherwise I wouldn't finish in five minutes but I would like to try to do my best to accommodate the Court's concerns about time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have no difficulty with taking an early break but how much -- how much would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Certainly no more than 15 minutes but I'm going to try to be less than that if I can. So that's what I'll try to do during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will have a break for half an hour and resume at 10.55.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to introduce to the Chamber Flavia Romiti, an intern from Rome, Italy, who is joining us for this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably Mr. Tieger should introduce the new team member.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, in this case, someone who needs no introduction to the Bench, Mr. Mr. McCloskey will be assisting us with the next examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. McCloskey. Yes, please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We will need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Finally, Witness, I wanted to show you one last document, that's 65 ter 24968, and direct your attention to the second page in B/C/S, the second-to-last paragraph on that page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, let's go into closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecutor's microphone please be switched off?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Witness, here I have a statement of Mr. Fadil Banjanovic. The ERN number is 0217378.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we briefly go into closed session? [In English] could we go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page, I think, 21?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Pavlovic submit a report to anyone in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he submitted the report or not. In any case, he was frequently invited to attend the sessions of the interim government.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How do you interpret an item in this document which states that he informed the Federal Secretariat of National Defence? I think we find it in -- I think it was on the page that was shown and admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it not the last --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Marko Pavlovic. Let me find it in the Serbian. Yes, there it is. Number 10. Major Marko Pavlovic informed the security and intelligence service about the execution. Did you know that he was reporting to the Federal Secretariat for National Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know he was reporting to them. A moment ago, when examined by the Prosecutor, I stated my conviction that he did belong to one of the federal security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 13, there was discussion about whether they were forced to leave, the Muslims, that is. Were the authorities part of that coercion, so to say? Did it exert pressure or why were they forced to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the interim government, they certainly did not coerce these people, but the circumstances under which these people lived were more than bad. It is these circumstances that forced people to move. If speaking of any kind of coercion, in terms of people coercing them, then it is the paramilitaries who often arrested people there and did other things that caused great fear among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 5, it was put to you that Radmilo Bogdanovic, minister of the interior of Serbia, or Yugoslavia, was the person in question. In 1994, was Mr. Bogdanovic minister?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was minister, but it was Mr. Bogdanovic in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that Mr. Bogdanovic resigned after the demonstrations in 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, on page 89, the following was put to you, that there were no conditions for dividing Zvornik because of the fact that it was mixed, was Bosnia as a whole mixed, and were there conditions for it to secede from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnia was mixed, and the former Yugoslavia was also mixed. The secession of Bosnia from Yugoslavia was a very risky option because three peoples live in Bosnia. Before this state was reformed, it was not possible to speak about any kind of democratic secession from the former federal state.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. An ethnic map was shown to you, and symbols or, rather, circles and dots depict the ethnic distribution there. We'll try to find the map that will display this more accurately. Can you tell us whether the Serbs took over the entire municipality of Zvornik? Are there two municipalities of Zvornik today and who controlled what during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs did not take over the entire municipality of Zvornik. To this day, there is a Muslim part of the municipality around Sapna, and it functions, it rather has functioned from the beginning of the war until this day. That is the Muslim municipality of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. 1D0672, could we please have that? While we are waiting, do you remember what our position was with regard to life together, and do you remember the agreement with the Muslims, with Zulfikarpasic and the panel discussion that he and I had in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember from the very beginning from when the multi-party elections were held in Bosnia, when a government was formed on the basis of consensus reached by the three peoples then. I remember full well everything that preceded the war. As for Bosnia leaving the former Yugoslavia, the Serbs in Bosnia asked that Bosnia be reorganised, either to have an assembly with two Chambers where the Chamber of peoples or nations would exercise a right of veto and also to prescribe which decisions had to be reached at assembly level, or the other proposal was to have a different kind of organisation like Switzerland, and on that basis Bosnia could be separated from the former state. Also, there were attempts, I remember that very well, with Zulfikarpasic to achieve an agreement that could peacefully resolve the situation; that is to say, Bosnia would either remain within the former Yugoslavia, and people would go on living the way they had lived until then, or to have this regionalisation carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. You were following developments in terms of the Lisbon agreement based on the Cutileiro Plan. Did Izetbegovic have the right to ask for independence after he had betrayed our conditio sine qua non? That is to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where are we heading? Is this arising from the line of cross-examination of Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellency. Mr. Tieger disputed the right to divide Zvornik because it's mixed and there would be minorities. However, as for what is Izetbegovic asked for, a million and a half Serbs would be a minority. If that would be a problem in Zvornik, it would have been far greater a problem in all of Bosnia. But let us enlarge the upper right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, that wasn't what the cross-examination was about. I didn't dispute the so-called right to divide Zvornik one way or another. I asked about the practical -- the practical consequences and the possibilities of doing so, and based on what the witness had previously said which was about the intermixed nature of Zvornik. Now, the accused is going into a political justification apparently for what in fact happened in Zvornik, which was -- which does not arise from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber agrees with Mr. Tieger. I don't have to tell you that your time is limited and use it in a wise manner. Please continue. I'm telling you to move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, would you like the witness to mark Muslim and Serb areas on this map which is different from the other one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the witness please be assisted with a pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, would you please mark this -- or, rather, you see the municipality of Zvornik. You see this thick line. Could you put a circle there around Serb areas and Muslim areas that are separate municipalities nowadays as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see here exactly where the boundaries of the municipality of Zvornik are.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Never mind. Let's give up on this altogether, then.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But definitely what can be seen here is the following: If the blue areas are Serb areas and the green ones are Muslim areas, then it's not necessary to draw a boundary line. It's obvious what it's like.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And who has more areas with an ethnic majority?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as far as areas in the municipality of Zvornik are concerned, it is the Serbs who had more land, but as far as population goes, there were more Muslims. But the Serbs owned more of the land there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. We can have this removed now. We are going to do more drawing some other time. On page 87, it was suggested to you, or cited, that the Serb Municipality of Zvornik wanted to take over control on the ground. On the 14th of February, 1992, was the Serb Municipality of Zvornik supposed to take over Muslim territories and the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not the objective. The objective of establishing the Serb Municipality of Zvornik was just like the objective of creating the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to reach a proper agreement on the peaceful transformation of Bosnia-Herzegovina in order to avoid a conflict and war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 81, what was quoted to you was that the Crisis Staff had declared a state of war. In relation to the then-existing Law on People's Defence and Self-Protection, could the municipality declare a state of war, a mobilisation, in a situation when it did not have any connections with the federal government?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It may be -- I mean, it is Mr. Karadzic's time, but the choices he's making can be -- have been commented on repeatedly by the Court. In this case, however, the reference to that was simply to place the witness contextually in the context of his statement that was a reference to the paragraph at which he discussed certain things so that was a passing reference to his statement in order to move on to a question about the time that particular time period. It wasn't in any way about that event, and this issue does not arose from cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that statement is fair enough.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The decisions, then, that were made by the provisional authorities or the interim government, were they against the law or the Law on National Defence, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, according to the Law of the former Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the municipalities and local communes made their own plans of defence and self-protection and they could operate within their own areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 78, you were reminded, Mr. Tieger reminded you, that on the 18th of March --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yesterday. [Interpretation] Yesterday's transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He reminded you that on the 28th March, agreement was reached regarding the Cutileiro Plan, the Lisbon agreement. Was that the first agreement in this regard, and do you remember when it was agreed for the first time that basically in principle there would be three Bosnias?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In February, as far as I can remember, 1992, and that preceded the Lisbon agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 75, it was suggested to you that the Crisis Staff was established on the basis of instructions. Muslims and Croats did they receive instructions from the SDS when they established their own Crisis Staffs, or, rather, who was the first to establish Crisis Staffs and when were Crisis Staffs established generally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know in the municipality of Zvornik, the Muslims established their Crisis Staff in the month of December 1991, and actually Crisis Staffs are bodies in which one can obtain information fast and people can assemble their people who are supposed to make a decision. It's a smaller body consultative that can act in five or ten minutes in a crisis situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would a Crisis Staff be established -- or rather, were instructions of crucial importance for establishing Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: An instruction was not crucial in that regard. It was the circumstances involved that were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Also, it was suggested to you -- or, rather, it was stated from some statement of yours that the secretary from the SDS was always in a position to establish communication with the field. Can you tell us whether there is any time difference there, difference in terms of periods of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There must be. From the establishment until the outbreak of the war, there were different periods of time. When there would be a crisis situation, then activity would be intensified and if not it would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Although the work of the party was frozen, what were communications like during the first year of the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the first year of the war, it was exceptionally difficult to communicate. Up until April 1992, it somehow did work but from April onwards, say until September, it was rather difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And let us conclude. Were you in a position to see for yourself what my views were regarding crimes against civilians, any civilians, but especially Muslim and Croat civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the beginning of the war, this was your first position, you signed that order that all prisoners of war, civilians, should be treated in accordance with the Geneva Conventions, all members of parliament knew that and all military personnel received that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And apart from the order itself, in various contacts, did you know what my positions were and what my efforts were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, your position was that the authorities should not exert any pressure against people, that they should help them whenever they can and that people should have a normal life ensured for them, if at all possible, but if circumstances required that somebody leave, then they should be enabled to leave, of course without any kind of pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the agreement with Zulfikarpasic, would we have lived together with Muslims in Bosnia and in Yugoslavia had that come into being?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we would have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you coming to a close, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you know that I or any other relevant person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your question starting with "did you know that," it must be leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did I or anybody from the Serbian community in Bosnia-Herzegovina have the intention or take measures to expel Muslims and Croats from our areas or possibly display a genocidal intentions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was my reaction when I learned that the people from Kozluk had left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You were very sorry about it and you were disappointed. In the talks that followed, I noticed that you were sorry to hear of any mass departure of population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did I ever support crimes against Muslims or Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I haven't heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And my last question, Witness: Did you know what kind of measures I took against paramilitaries specifically in your municipality, but more generally too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you played an important part in sending that unit that arrested the paramilitaries. Moreover, the appointment of Commander Pandurevic was a good stabilising measure for the Zvornik area because as a result nobody who carried arms could move about the municipality uncontrolled.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I raise one question arising from the last couple of questions in connection with sending in -- in connection with the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why wasn't that covered on cross-examination? That's mentioned in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, there is lots of things that -- I obviously have to make a judgement call about what to do in cross-examination, given the time. This is now specifically referenced. I just want to raise one point in that regard because Mr. Karadzic specifically focused on it as a matter arising out of cross, kind of funny to say he's able to redirect about matters arising out of cross and then claim that I can't go into it because it didn't arise in cross. A little bit paradoxical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will allow you to put the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Further cross-examination by Mr. Tieger:

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In connection with Mr. Karadzic's last question about the measures he took against paramilitaries in Zvornik, you were aware, Witness, were you not, that the action taken against paramilitaries only occurred after Minister of Information Ostojic was stopped and abused at a check-point and complained very angrily about that -- angrily and publicly about that at, among other things I think you indicated, an assembly session; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one of the incidents that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I contribute to more precision? It follows from this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one question, Mr. Karadzic. Further re-examination by Mr. Karadzic:

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was that a decisive incident and was it only then that the preparations for the arrest of the paramilitaries began?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KW317 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The preparations began much earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Witness. On behalf of the Chamber, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. You are free to go, but we will rise all together. We will take a break now for 45 minutes and resume at 10 past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to introduce to the Chamber Beatris Spasova from Bulgaria who is working as an intern for our team and will join us this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. I have with me today Edward Jeremy to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Would the witness make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovcanin, please be seated and make yourself comfortable. So if the counsel representing Mr. Borovcanin could introduce herself?

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, Tatjana Cmeric appearing today for Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Borovcanin, probably you are well aware of this, but before you commence your evidence I must draw your attention to a certain rule that we have here at the Tribunal. That is Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, from the Prosecution or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. However, in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled in such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge, I understood, but I request additional clarification. Does this pertain only to this Tribunal or to all courts in the world?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I should say it's -- that includes all courts in the world.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know if there were ranks at your time and I don't know which rank you held, I will only address you as Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you give a statement to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you for pausing. That's how we should continue and speak slowly for everything to be recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we get 1D07375A?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin, do you see that statement of yours before you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. This is the first page. This is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you read and sign this statement?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us show the last page to the witness for him to identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There is no need to correct anything, right, to correct any information such as dates and what have you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Everything is all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to ask you the same questions today in this courtroom, would your answers essentially be the same?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this statement under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are four associated exhibits. We would ask that each of them be added to our 65 ter list as we hadn't interviewed Mr. Borovcanin at the time we filed that list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, do you have any objection to the admission of Rule 92 ter statement as well as associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, the only item that I am concerned about is the third one, which appears in para 13. I'm not sure if it is relevant. Having said that, the document -- the statement can be understood without the document as well. So the statement as well as the other three documents will be admitted. Shall we assign the numbers now?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The 92 ter statement will be Exhibit D3659; 65 ter 03815 will be Exhibit D3660; 65 ter 03816 will be Exhibit D3661; and 65 ter 04736 will be Exhibit D3662.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read out a short summary of Mr. Ljubomir Borovcanin's statement in English. [In English] Ljubomir Borovcanin was deputy commander of the Special Police Brigade of the Republika Srpska Ministry of Interior during July 1995. On 10th of July, 1995, while engaged in the Sarajevo battlefield he received an order designating him as commander of a MUP unit to be dispatched to the area of Srebrenica. On 13th of July, 1995, Mr. Borovcanin was joined in Bratunac by the journalist Zoran Petrovic who accompanied him during his movement over the next two days and recorded some of the events. Sometime before 4.00 p.m. on 13th of July, 1995, Mr. Borovcanin was in the Sandici area when General Mladic addressed the Bosnian Muslim prisoners who were gathered there. Mr. Borovcanin heard General Mladic tell them that they were waiting for buses and that they would be transported to their families in Kladanj and Tuzla. He believed that General Mladic was sincere and that this was what would happen. He knew of no plan to kill prisoners. Later that afternoon, as Mr. Borovcanin was driving from Sandici towards Zvornik, he was informed over a Motorola that something terrible had happened at the -- and that he should return. When he returned and passed by the Kravica warehouse, he observed about 20 to 30 bodies laying on the ground in front of the warehouse building. He stopped on the road just past the warehouse and at the junction of the road and the driveway into the warehouse. He was told that one of the Muslim prisoners grabbed -- had grabbed a police officer's rifle and killed him. He was also told that another officer had then struggled to take the rifle from the prisoner and that his hands burned in the process. He was also told that some Muslim prisoners had been killed as a result of this incident and those were the bodies that he had seen. Mr. Borovcanin reported the incident to the Bratunac Brigade of the VRS. Later that evening, he spoke with Miroslav Deronjic, who had been appointed civilian commissioner for Srebrenica, about what had happened at the Kravica warehouse. On 14th of July, 1995, Mr. Borovcanin also discussed the incident with Deputy Minister of Interior Tomo Kovac. On 15th of July, 1995, he went to the Zvornik Brigade command.
